name: Virgin Islands National Park
blurb: Reefs, seagrass bays and dry forest on St. John, where urchins guard the reef.

tip.title: Lose the sea urchins
tip.text: Long-spined urchins graze algae on the reef. Set Long-spined sea urchin to -100% and watch algae spread, then the hawksbills that eat urchins.

sources.title: National Park Service: Virgin Islands nature

notes: The story and why it matters come from the Wikipedia articles listed below (Virgin Islands National Park, Hawksbill sea turtle, Diadema antillarum). Individual species and links have not been checked one by one. Feeding links that match a GloBI (Global Biotic Interactions) record are marked in the node details, with a link to the records. A few links were added from GloBI records.

nodes.desc: Clear shallow water and open slopes let light reach seagrass, algae and the dry-forest canopy.
Warm, low-nutrient Caribbean water stays clear, so light reaches the seagrass beds and reefs that ring the island.
Shallow soil on the mountainous island holds the dry forest and is replenished by decomposed leaves.

nodes.name: Bacteria and fungi
nodes.desc: Break down dead seagrass, algae and leaf litter and return nutrients to the sand and soil.
Seagrass that covers the sea floor of bays such as Maho Bay and Salt Pond Bay. Green turtles and queen conch graze it.
A calcified green alga of reefs and sand. Parrotfish, urchins and turtles graze algae like it.
Drifting algae in the open water. They feed zooplankton and, through them, schooling fish.

nodes.name: Dry forest trees
nodes.desc: Gumbo-limbo is a typical tree of the dry to moist forest that covers the island hills. Deer and iguanas browse such foliage.
Tiny grazers of phytoplankton that feed sardines and other small fish.
Grazes algae on reefs. A disease killed over 97% of Caribbean Diadema in 1983, and algae then overgrew many reefs.
Scrapes algae from rock and coral, keeping reefs from being overgrown, and excretes the ground rock as sand.
A large sea snail that grazes algae and seagrass in sandy meadows. It is an important food for turtles and nurse sharks.
Grazes seagrass beds and algae. Sea turtles are seen at Maho Bay.
The most recorded land mammal near the park. It browses leaves and shoots of the dry forest.
A big leaf-eating lizard of the island forest, preyed on by birds and mammals when young.
A plunge-diving fish eater, and one of the park's Important Bird Area species.
The most recorded bird near the park. It snatches fish, squid and jellyfish from the surface and steals food from other seabirds.
An introduced predator of lizards, birds and eggs, including sea turtle nests.
A top marine predator of the Caribbean that hunts sea turtles among many other prey.

story: Virgin Islands National Park preserves about 60% of the land on Saint John, more than 5,500 acres of adjacent ocean, and nearly all of Hassel Island. It is well known for snorkeling and diving, and has miles of trails through tropical rainforest.
matters: Laurance Rockefeller's Jackson Hole Preserve donated its land in 1956 on condition that it be protected from development. After hurricanes Irma and Maria in 2017, visits fell from 304,408 in 2017 to 112,287 in 2018.
